CloudDesk Technologies
 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
1. Authority, scope and ownership
SYNTHETIC / DEMO - document control
CD-BDR-001 | Version 1.0 (wording revision). Proposed effective date: 2026-10-22. Planned next review:
2027-10-22. These dates are proposals, not an approved schedule. Owner and coordinator: Engineering
Lead. Accountable approver: CTO; approval not recorded. Review annually and after material changes,
incidents or exercises.
Status and limits
CloudDesk Technologies is a fictional 75-person B2B SaaS vendor. This model-authored policy sets proposed
SYNTHETIC / DEMO requirements, not operating facts. Review_status: requires_user_review. It provides no
evidence of deployed backup schedules, implemented controls, actual restore tests or successful recoveries.
It makes no SLA, certification or legal compliance claim. It assumes no live contact directory, staffed recovery
team or guaranteed response time.
Scope and ownership
This policy covers customer databases, tenant objects and attachments. It also covers production
configuration, infrastructure definitions, scoped logs, SaaS dependencies and recovery documentation.
System owners must identify authoritative data, dependencies, exclusions and recovery procedures. Platform
Engineering must implement the technical controls assigned to it once approved. The Engineering Lead must
coordinate inventories, tests and remediation. The CTO must approve objectives, resources and residual risk.
Verify coverage for each asset before adoption; this document is not a backup inventory.
Related policy authority
Use access_control_policy.pdf for access requirements, encryption_key_management_policy.pdf
(CD-ENC-001) for encryption and keys, information_security_policy.pdf (CD-ISP-001) for security governance,
and incident_response_plan.pdf (CD-IRP-001) for incident response. These policies remain authoritative in
their areas. Apply the recovery requirements here without weakening them. Record any conflict and have the
Engineering Lead and CTO resolve it before adoption.

Page 2
CloudDesk Technologies
 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
2. Inventory, impact assessment and proposed schedules
Backup inventory and classification
For each dataset, record the system owner, source, business purpose, tenant scope and highest applicable
classification: Public, Internal, Confidential or Restricted under CD-ISP-001. Record the backup method,
location/account/region, copy dependencies, key identifier/version, authorized restore role, vendor and
runbook. Include coverage gaps, exclusions, deletion behavior, verification method, holds and the approval
status of proposed frequency and retention. Keep secret key material and credentials out of the backup
inventory.
Business impact analysis and objectives
System owners must prepare a business impact analysis (BIA) before recovery objectives are committed.
Assess outage harm over time, data-loss tolerance, customer and contractual obligations, dependency
failures, staffing, costs and recovery order. The Engineering Lead must review assumptions and feasibility.
The CTO approves recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO) after this assessment.
RTO is the time to restore service; RPO is the tolerable loss of recent data. Both remain TBD pending BIA,
business and contractual review. This policy provides no numerical targets or availability guarantees.
Proposed frequency and retention - TBD
Backup frequency and retention are TBD pending BIA/business and contractual review. Owners must propose
risk-based values for each dataset, considering change rate, sensitivity, loss tolerance, recovery cost and
obligations. The Engineering Lead must review them and the CTO must approve them before deployment.
Record approved values and their rationale separately. No daily, weekly or other deployed schedule or fixed
retention period is asserted. Assess snapshots and replication for recoverability independently: replication can
propagate corruption and does not by itself prove that a backup can be recovered.
Retention, holds and disposal
Reconcile backup expiry with customer deletion commitments, legal or incident holds and vendor deletion
behavior, using appropriate advice. Record delayed deletion in retained copies and prevent deleted data from
being unintentionally reintroduced during restore. Restrict held copies and their keys. Dispose of them only
after approved retention has ended and holds have been released; keep disposal evidence. Preserve the
separate minimum 12-month retention for KMS audit logs. That minimum is not a backup retention period or a
rule for all records.

[mandatory_document_context; backup_disaster_recovery_policy.pdf:p3]

Page 3

 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
3. Encryption, keys and backup protection
Encryption and grant separation
Encrypt all production backups and snapshots at rest with AES-256 and protect transfers with TLS 1.2 or TLS
1.3. Use managed KMS and backup-specific key grants separate from ordinary application access. Keep
key-encryption keys non-exportable in KMS. Separate key administration from routine data access; key
administrators receive no default decrypt permission. The Engineering Lead must approve grants. Use unique
user accounts and multi-factor authentication for administrative access. Review permissions and key grants
every quarter and revoke terminated employee access within 24 hours.
Key versions and recoverability
Rotate symmetric key-encryption keys at least every 12 months under CD-ENC-001. Rotation alone does not
re-encrypt historical data. Keep older key versions under restricted access for the full lifetime of dependent
retained backups, including legal or incident holds. Record KMS availability, account, region, identity and
version dependencies, and verify authorized decrypt access during restore checks. Never destroy a key just
because the active version has rotated. Destruction requires Engineering Lead and CTO approval, evidence
that dependent retention has ended, recovery checks showing no remaining need, and a destruction record.
Compromise and emergency access
For suspected key compromise, immediately open an incident, revoke affected identity grants and disable
compromised key versions where safe. Create replacement keys. Assess exposure, historical re-encryption
and backup recoverability before taking destructive action. The CTO must authorize temporary emergency
decrypt access, with logging and next-business-day review. Use trusted identities and recovery paths; do not
reconnect compromised grants to restore data. Review KMS administrative and decrypt audit events monthly
and after incidents. Retain those logs for at least 12 months in restricted encrypted storage.
Proposed isolation and immutability controls
Choose backup protections according to risk. Options include separate recovery identities and restricted
permission to delete backups. Consider isolated backup accounts or separate systems that would not fail
together. Provider-supported immutable copies (protected from change or deletion) or offline copies are
options where justified by risk. Before adoption, the Engineering Lead must technically verify how the provider
applies these protections, including retention locks, recovery access and cost. Test whether control of
production would let an attacker alter backups or keys. Escalate shared failure paths and document
compensating safeguards. No immutable backup, air gap, separate-region copy, geo-replication or
ransomware resistance is asserted as implemented.

[mandatory_document_context; backup_disaster_recovery_policy.pdf:p4]
SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 4
CloudDesk Technologies
 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
4. Disaster activation and safe restoration
Declaration and alternate communications
The Engineering Lead must assess disruption, affected tenants, available dependencies and likely recovery
needs using CD-IRP-001 severity rules. Escalate critical service loss, destructive activity or key/backup
compromise promptly to the CTO. The CTO must authorize disaster declaration, material service shutdowns,
resources and material residual risk. Record the scope, rationale, time and delegated authority. Follow the
incident plan for urgent reversible containment. If normal accounts or messaging are unavailable or suspect,
use separately verified alternate contacts and a restricted decision log. A human reviewer must validate
contacts and substitutes before adoption.
Dependency-led restoration sequence
System owners must document a dependency graph and propose a restoration sequence. First establish
trusted identity, administrative access, network and KMS connectivity. Then recover validated infrastructure
and configuration, restore consistent databases and objects, and reconcile queues, indexes and dependent
services. Validate and reconnect in phases. This sequence is a planning aid, not a claim about deployed
architecture. Before each step, confirm vendor prerequisites, clean credentials, backup availability, key
versions and the recovery environment. Record recovery points and dependencies. Pause if prerequisite
integrity or authorized decrypt access cannot be established.
Safe recovery after a cyber incident
Coordinate containment, evidence preservation and eradication under CD-IRP-001. Assess the compromise
window and backup provenance. Select a recovery point outside known corruption and record uncertainty.
Scan and restore in isolation with trusted tools and rebuilt systems. Remove persistence and replace
compromised credentials. A recent or decryptable backup is not proof that it is safe. Preserve incident
evidence where safe; do not overwrite originals or blindly destroy keys. The Engineering Lead verifies
containment. The CTO approves material residual risk and the return of critical service.
Tenant integrity and service gates
Before reconnection, system owners must verify hashes or application-level integrity, transactional
consistency, tenant boundaries, permissions, schema compatibility, deletion/hold reconciliation and
representative customer workflows. Reconcile replayed events and duplicate writes without exposing one
tenant to another. Record gaps, actual elapsed time and the recoverable data point. Compare these with
approved objectives when available; do not promise an unapproved RTO/RPO. Define phased monitoring,
rollback and stop criteria. Failed checks or returning indicators must stop release and reopen the investigation.
External communications require CTO authorization and a case-specific notification assessment.

[mandatory_document_context; backup_disaster_recovery_policy.pdf:p5]
SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 5
CloudDesk Technologies
 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
5. Restore testing, continuity exercises and dependencies
Representative quarterly encrypted restore tests
Test a representative encrypted restore at least quarterly. Record data integrity, authorized key access and
the recovery outcome. Plan risk-based coverage across datasets, backup types and key versions over
successive tests; this does not require restoring every backup each quarter. Use isolated environments and
synthetic data where feasible. Restrict handling of any necessary customer data. Record the source/backup
ID, recovery point, key version, operator authorization, checks, elapsed time, failures and limitations. Compare
results with approved objectives. A test is not an SLA or proof that every system can be recovered.
Negative recovery scenarios and remediation
Exercise missing or disabled keys, denied decrypt grants, unavailable KMS or providers, corrupted or
incomplete copies, inconsistent database/object recovery points, compromised credentials and cross-tenant
access attempts. Responders must stop unsafe restoration, preserve evidence and escalate to the
Engineering Lead and CTO. Use a validated alternative or document that recovery is not possible. Never
bypass authorization or suppress failed integrity checks. Assign each finding an owner and due date, and keep
retest evidence. Extracting text from this policy is not a restoration test.
Annual continuity exercises are separate
Exercise continuity scenarios at least annually and after material changes under CD-ISP-001, and coordinate
incident exercises under CD-IRP-001. Cover unavailable responders, alternate communications, cloud or
identity outages, vendor failure, ransomware, customer impact and decision authority. Record participants,
assumptions, decisions, gaps and corrective actions. An annual tabletop does not replace a representative
quarterly encrypted restore. A restore test alone does not satisfy the broader annual continuity exercise. No
exercise or restoration is claimed completed.
Vendor and shared dependencies
System owners must assess cloud storage, KMS, identity, DNS, SaaS exports, support availability, regional
dependencies and provider recovery/deletion limitations. Assess vendors before use. The Engineering Lead
must review the assessment; the CTO must accept material residual risk. Reassess critical vendors annually
and after material changes or incidents. Verify contracts, export portability, recovery responsibilities, contacts
and exit dependencies. Provider replication, assurances or advertised recovery targets do not establish
CloudDesk recoverability. Record inaccessible vendor data and recovery gaps in the risk register.

[mandatory_document_context; backup_disaster_recovery_policy.pdf:p6]
SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 6
CloudDesk Technologies
 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
6. Changes, exceptions and review evidence
Change approval and risk governance
Before material changes to architecture, backup methods, retention, keys, vendors or recovery runbooks,
system owners must assess the effect on coverage and recoverability. The Engineering Lead must review
dependencies, validation and rollback. The CTO must approve material risk and revised objectives before
adoption. Update inventories and runbooks and record validation evidence. Assess risks at least annually,
before material service changes and before onboarding scoped vendors. Review open risks quarterly. The
CTO must accept residual risk; escalate overdue high-impact actions.
Exceptions and emergency deviations
Before deviating, the owner must record affected assets/data, the requirement, rationale, risk, compensating
safeguards, responsible owner and expiry. The Engineering Lead must assess the request and the CTO must
approve or reject it. Exceptions expire within 90 days and must be reviewed monthly. Renewal requires a fresh
assessment and approval. Emergency deviations require an incident record and CTO review by the next
business day. CD-ENC-001 remains authoritative for encryption exceptions and destructive key approvals.
This policy supplies no active exception or approval.
Expected evidence artifacts
Keep the backup inventory and coverage map. Keep the BIA and objective approvals, along with proposed
and approved schedules and retention.
Keep configuration and access/grant reviews. Keep backup job outcomes and failure escalations, key-version
dependency checks, restore reports and integrity results.
Keep continuity exercise findings, incident decisions and vendor assessments. Keep change and exception
approvals and corrective-action closure evidence. Restrict access to records and maintain ownership, version
history, approved retention and holds. No completed evidence artifacts are supplied. Preserve the minimum
12-month retention for KMS audit logs without applying that minimum to all records.
Human review and adoption gate
Before adoption, human reviewers must validate staffing, substitutes, declaration authority, inventories,
proposed isolation and immutability, key access and recoverability, vendor limitations, BIA, customer
contracts, notification obligations and resource feasibility. The Engineering Lead must review this policy
annually and after material changes, incidents or exercises. Record reviewer feedback and CTO approval
before operational adoption. Approval_status: not_recorded; review_status: requires_user_review. This is a
proposed policy for a fictional company, not an approved recovery plan or compliance attestation.

Policy requirements do not establish adoption, approval, implementation or compliance. Human review required.

obligations. The Engineering Lead must review them and the CTO must approve them before deployment.
Record approved values and their rationale separately. No daily, weekly or other deployed schedule or fixed
retention period is asserted. Assess snapshots and replication for recoverability independently: replication can
propagate corruption and does not by itself prove that a backup can be recovered.
Retention, holds and disposal
Reconcile backup expiry with customer deletion commitments, legal or incident holds and vendor deletion
behavior, using appropriate advice. Record delayed deletion in retained copies and prevent deleted data from
being unintentionally reintroduced during restore. Restrict held copies and their keys. Dispose of them only
after approved retention has ended and holds have been released; keep disposal evidence. Preserve the
separate minimum 12-month retention for KMS audit logs. That minimum is not a backup retention period or a
rule for all records.

SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 3
CloudDesk Technologies

3. Encryption, keys and backup protection
Encryption and grant separation
Encrypt all production backups and snapshots at rest with AES-256 and protect transfers with TLS 1.2 or TLS
1.3. Use managed KMS and backup-specific key grants separate from ordinary application access. Keep
key-encryption keys non-exportable in KMS. Separate key administration from routine data access; key
administrators receive no default decrypt permission. The Engineering Lead must approve grants. Use unique
user accounts and multi-factor authentication for administrative access. Review permissions and key grants
every quarter and revoke terminated employee access within 24 hours.
Key versions and recoverability
Rotate symmetric key-encryption keys at least every 12 months under CD-ENC-001. Rotation alone does not
re-encrypt historical data. Keep older key versions under restricted access for the full lifetime of dependent
retained backups, including legal or incident holds. Record KMS availability, account, region, identity and
version dependencies, and verify authorized decrypt access during restore checks. Never destroy a key just
because the active version has rotated. Destruction requires Engineering Lead and CTO approval, evidence
that dependent retention has ended, recovery checks showing no remaining need, and a destruction record.
Compromise and emergency access
For suspected key compromise, immediately open an incident, revoke affected identity grants and disable
compromised key versions where safe. Create replacement keys. Assess exposure, historical re-encryption
and backup recoverability before taking destructive action. The CTO must authorize temporary emergency
decrypt access, with logging and next-business-day review. Use trusted identities and recovery paths; do not
reconnect compromised grants to restore data. Review KMS administrative and decrypt audit events monthly
and after incidents. Retain those logs for at least 12 months in restricted encrypted storage.
Proposed isolation and immutability controls
Choose backup protections according to risk. Options include separate recovery identities and restricted
permission to delete backups. Consider isolated backup accounts or separate systems that would not fail
together. Provider-supported immutable copies (protected from change or deletion) or offline copies are
options where justified by risk. Before adoption, the Engineering Lead must technically verify how the provider
applies these protections, including retention locks, recovery access and cost. Test whether control of
production would let an attacker alter backups or keys. Escalate shared failure paths and document
compensating safeguards. No immutable backup, air gap, separate-region copy, geo-replication or
ransomware resistance is asserted as implemented.

SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 4
CloudDesk Technologies

4. Disaster activation and safe restoration
Declaration and alternate communications
The Engineering Lead must assess disruption, affected tenants, available dependencies and likely recovery
needs using CD-IRP-001 severity rules. Escalate critical service loss, destructive activity or key/backup
compromise promptly to the CTO. The CTO must authorize disaster declaration, material service shutdowns,
resources and material residual risk. Record the scope, rationale, time and delegated authority. Follow the
incident plan for urgent reversible containment. If normal accounts or messaging are unavailable or suspect,
use separately verified alternate contacts and a restricted decision log. A human reviewer must validate
contacts and substitutes before adoption.
Dependency-led restoration sequence
System owners must document a dependency graph and propose a restoration sequence. First establish
trusted identity, administrative access, network and KMS connectivity. Then recover validated infrastructure
and configuration, restore consistent databases and objects, and reconcile queues, indexes and dependent
services. Validate and reconnect in phases. This sequence is a planning aid, not a claim about deployed
architecture. Before each step, confirm vendor prerequisites, clean credentials, backup availability, key
versions and the recovery environment. Record recovery points and dependencies. Pause if prerequisite
integrity or authorized decrypt access cannot be established.
Safe recovery after a cyber incident
Coordinate containment, evidence preservation and eradication under CD-IRP-001. Assess the compromise
window and backup provenance. Select a recovery point outside known corruption and record uncertainty.
Scan and restore in isolation with trusted tools and rebuilt systems. Remove persistence and replace
compromised credentials. A recent or decryptable backup is not proof that it is safe. Preserve incident
evidence where safe; do not overwrite originals or blindly destroy keys. The Engineering Lead verifies
containment. The CTO approves material residual risk and the return of critical service.
Tenant integrity and service gates
Before reconnection, system owners must verify hashes or application-level integrity, transactional
consistency, tenant boundaries, permissions, schema compatibility, deletion/hold reconciliation and
representative customer workflows. Reconcile replayed events and duplicate writes without exposing one
tenant to another. Record gaps, actual elapsed time and the recoverable data point. Compare these with
approved objectives when available; do not promise an unapproved RTO/RPO. Define phased monitoring,
rollback and stop criteria. Failed checks or returning indicators must stop release and reopen the investigation.
External communications require CTO authorization and a case-specific notification assessment.

SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 5
CloudDesk Technologies
 Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy
5. Restore testing, continuity exercises and dependencies
Representative quarterly encrypted restore tests
Test a representative encrypted restore at least quarterly. Record data integrity, authorized key access and
the recovery outcome. Plan risk-based coverage across datasets, backup types and key versions over
successive tests; this does not require restoring every backup each quarter. Use isolated environments and
synthetic data where feasible. Restrict handling of any necessary customer data. Record the source/backup
ID, recovery point, key version, operator authorization, checks, elapsed time, failures and limitations. Compare
results with approved objectives. A test is not an SLA or proof that every system can be recovered.
Negative recovery scenarios and remediation
Exercise missing or disabled keys, denied decrypt grants, unavailable KMS or providers, corrupted or
incomplete copies, inconsistent database/object recovery points, compromised credentials and cross-tenant
access attempts. Responders must stop unsafe restoration, preserve evidence and escalate to the
Engineering Lead and CTO. Use a validated alternative or document that recovery is not possible. Never
bypass authorization or suppress failed integrity checks. Assign each finding an owner and due date, and keep
retest evidence. Extracting text from this policy is not a restoration test.
Annual continuity exercises are separate
Exercise continuity scenarios at least annually and after material changes under CD-ISP-001, and coordinate
incident exercises under CD-IRP-001. Cover unavailable responders, alternate communications, cloud or
identity outages, vendor failure, ransomware, customer impact and decision authority. Record participants,
assumptions, decisions, gaps and corrective actions. An annual tabletop does not replace a representative
quarterly encrypted restore. A restore test alone does not satisfy the broader annual continuity exercise. No
exercise or restoration is claimed completed.
Vendor and shared dependencies
System owners must assess cloud storage, KMS, identity, DNS, SaaS exports, support availability, regional
dependencies and provider recovery/deletion limitations. Assess vendors before use. The Engineering Lead
must review the assessment; the CTO must accept material residual risk. Reassess critical vendors annually
and after material changes or incidents. Verify contracts, export portability, recovery responsibilities, contacts
and exit dependencies. Provider replication, assurances or advertised recovery targets do not establish
CloudDesk recoverability. Record inaccessible vendor data and recovery gaps in the risk register.

Page 6
CloudDesk Technologies

6. Changes, exceptions and review evidence
Change approval and risk governance
Before material changes to architecture, backup methods, retention, keys, vendors or recovery runbooks,
system owners must assess the effect on coverage and recoverability. The Engineering Lead must review
dependencies, validation and rollback. The CTO must approve material risk and revised objectives before
adoption. Update inventories and runbooks and record validation evidence. Assess risks at least annually,
before material service changes and before onboarding scoped vendors. Review open risks quarterly. The
CTO must accept residual risk; escalate overdue high-impact actions.
Exceptions and emergency deviations
Before deviating, the owner must record affected assets/data, the requirement, rationale, risk, compensating
safeguards, responsible owner and expiry. The Engineering Lead must assess the request and the CTO must
approve or reject it. Exceptions expire within 90 days and must be reviewed monthly. Renewal requires a fresh
assessment and approval. Emergency deviations require an incident record and CTO review by the next
business day. CD-ENC-001 remains authoritative for encryption exceptions and destructive key approvals.
This policy supplies no active exception or approval.
Expected evidence artifacts
Keep the backup inventory and coverage map. Keep the BIA and objective approvals, along with proposed
and approved schedules and retention.
Keep configuration and access/grant reviews. Keep backup job outcomes and failure escalations, key-version
dependency checks, restore reports and integrity results.

history, approved retention and holds. No completed evidence artifacts are supplied. Preserve the minimum

Human review and adoption gate
Before adoption, human reviewers must validate staffing, substitutes, declaration authority, inventories,
proposed isolation and immutability, key access and recoverability, vendor limitations, BIA, customer

annually and after material changes, incidents or exercises. Record reviewer feedback and CTO approval
before operational adoption. Approval_status: not_recorded; review_status: requires_user_review. This is a
proposed policy for a fictional company, not an approved recovery plan or compliance attestation.

approves material residual risk and critical-service return under incident authority when applicable.

2. Reporting, classification and escalation
Proposed reporting routes
The proposed route is an access-restricted incident ticket and direct contact with the Engineering Lead
through a verified internal directory. These are proposals, not live services or monitored addresses. If
unavailable, contact the CTO or a designated substitute. If company accounts may be compromised, use a
separately verified alternate contact method. Validate contacts, coverage and escalation paths before
adoption. Report promptly when you discover a concern; do not wait for proof. Keep passwords, tokens and
unnecessary customer data out of reports.
Event versus incident
An event is an observation, such as a failed login, alert or outage, that needs assessment. An incident is
suspected or confirmed unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, destructive activity or disruption that
needs a coordinated response. The Engineering Lead records the classification and reasons, including false
positives and routine faults. If significant harm is uncertain, handle the case as a provisional incident. A lack of
confirmed exfiltration does not prove that no data was accessed.
Severity levels
SEV1 Critical: active widespread compromise, destructive cyber extortion, likely material customer data
exposure or sustained loss of a critical service. Escalate directly to the CTO and start coordinating technical
and continuity work immediately on recognition.
SEV2 High: credible privileged credential/key compromise, limited suspected customer exposure or significant
contained disruption. Inform the CTO promptly and assess the need for specialist help.
SEV3 Moderate: an incident limited to one system, with no current evidence of privileged access or customer
exposure. The Engineering Lead directs the response and informs the CTO if the scope grows.
SEV4 Low: a suspicious event or unsuccessful attempt with no identified impact. Record, assess and monitor
it; record the reasons before closing it.
Reassessment and handover
Severity can change. Raise it for active spread, sensitive data access, tenant boundary failures, evidence
tampering, key or backup compromise, uncertain containment, a growing outage or legal/contract notification

recoverability. Rotation alone does not re-encrypt historical data. Keep restricted older key versions while
retained data or backups need them. The CTO authorizes temporary emergency decrypt access, with logging
and next-business-day review. Destruction requires Engineering Lead and CTO approval after retention and
recovery checks. Never blindly delete keys to contain an incident.
Eradication and recovery gates

replacement credentials. Keep backup-specific key grants separate from ordinary application access. Before
restoring, assess backup integrity and the compromise window, scan in isolation, test authorized decrypt
access, and validate data, tenant separation and critical service behavior. System owners propose phased
reconnection, monitoring and rollback criteria. The Engineering Lead verifies containment. The CTO approves
material residual risk and the return of critical service. Follow approved RTO/RPO when established; this plan
guarantees no numerical targets. Reopen the investigation if indicators return.

Page 5
CloudDesk Technologies

5. Extortion, communications and notification decisions
Cyber extortion decisions
Treat ransomware, destructive threats and data-theft extortion as potential SEV1 incidents. Keep demands
and evidence, isolate affected paths, and protect clean backups and recovery credentials. Individual
responders must not negotiate, pay, promise secrecy or contact attackers. The CTO coordinates decisions
with qualified legal advice, appropriate leadership and relevant insurer/law-enforcement consultation where
applicable. Assess safety, sanctions and other applicable restrictions, contractual duties, recoverability and
alternatives. This plan pre-authorizes no payment. Payment or a decryption tool does not guarantee recovery,
deletion or confidentiality. Record decisions and independently validate any proposed recovery tool in
isolation.
Communication authorization
The Engineering Lead keeps a factual internal situation report covering known scope, uncertainty, actions
proposed or taken, and the next review. The CTO authorizes external/customer communications with relevant
legal/privacy advice and an assigned spokesperson. Responders must avoid speculation, attribution and
unapproved statements. Verify recipients and use secure alternate routes if normal messaging is affected.
Share sensitive indicators and personal data only with those who need them. Keep approved versions,
recipients and delivery evidence. This plan records no actual communication or notification.
Customer and external notification assessment
Assess customer contracts, provider terms, applicable laws and affected jurisdictions case by case with
qualified advice. Record when awareness arose, the decision owner, relevant duty/trigger, affected parties,
required content, deadline and calculation basis, uncertainty and approval. There is no universal notification
deadline in this plan. Do not wait for perfect attribution or a completed investigation when a duty requires
earlier notice. Track changing facts and supplemental updates. Record the reasons for notification or
non-notification. Consider regulators, affected individuals, customers, providers and law enforcement where
applicable; every incident does not require every recipient.
Continuity and customer support
Coordinate service status, workarounds, restoration priorities and support responses with system owners and
the CTO. Assess customer impacts and contractual recovery commitments without promising unverified
restoration times. Check that only authorized recovery roles can access backups and that recovery does not
reconnect compromised identities. Record disputed facts and decisions to defer recovery. Preserve required
holds and evidence during communications and restoration.

CTO reviews significant incidents and accepts material residual risk. Hold a blameless lessons-learned review

evidence. Add risks and overdue material actions to the risk register. Closure does not remove unresolved
obligations or evidence holds.

Inventory and accountable ownership

purpose, engagement dates and renewal/exit conditions. Map information classes, customer data categories,
processing purposes, privileges and interfaces. Identify storage, processing and support locations,
subprocessors and upstream dependencies. Track contract and assessment versions, risk tier and rationale,
findings, approvals, review dates, exit plans and evidence limitations. Update the inventory after material
changes and retirement. This sample supplies no actual vendor inventory.
Risk tiering dimensions
Assess customer data sensitivity and volume, processor/subprocessor roles, administrative or persistent
access, service criticality, resilience and recoverability. Consider geography/jurisdiction, cross-border
processing, concentration and substitutability. Identify shared cloud, identity, region and fourth-party failure
paths. Record inherent risk, verified safeguards and residual risk separately. Missing information requires
review; it is not evidence of low risk.
Proposed tiers and escalation
Classify vendors as high risk if they have privileged production access, process sensitive customer data, or
provide a critical dependency whose failure could cause material harm. Flag vendors essential to service or
recovery as critical, separately from their risk tier, to retain annual reassessment. Moderate risk means
bounded nonprivileged access to nonpublic information without high-risk characteristics. Low risk requires
documented limited exposure and low impact. The Engineering Lead reviews the rationale. Use the higher
applicable tier when dimensions conflict, and escalate unresolved uncertainty to the CTO.

Engineering Lead coordinates security risk assessments at least annually and open-risk reviews quarterly.
Record findings, remediation owners, due dates and CTO acceptance decisions. Escalate overdue material
risks rather than renewing silently.

through verified internal routes to be established before adoption. Use the CTO or a designated alternate if the

6. Exit, records, exceptions and adoption
Vendor offboarding and portability
Before critical use, plan exit triggers, alternative providers or manual options, export formats, ownership,
migration sequence, dependency validation, costs and contract assistance. Test portability proportionately
with authorized minimized or synthetic data. No successful migration is asserted. At termination, expiry or
scope reduction, remove access in time for the effective end and according to risk. Revoke vendor accounts,

safeguards, remediation owner and expiry. The Engineering Lead assesses the request; the CTO approves or

approval. Expired approval cannot authorize use. Emergency deviations require a linked incident and
next-business-day CTO review. Do not delay urgent containment. Exceptions cannot erase applicable
obligations or silently extend employee termination limits. Encryption and destructive key authority remain
unchanged. No active exception is asserted.

The Engineering Lead reviews this policy annually and after material changes or incidents. Before adoption,
human reviewers must validate tier criteria, inventory coverage, contract/privacy advice, evidence sufficiency,
staffing and substitutes, reporting routes, monitoring proposals, recovery dependencies and feasible exits
against all seven related policies. Record conflicts, feedback and CTO approval. Approval_status:
not_recorded; review_status: requires_user_review. This proposed policy does not establish that CloudDesk
has completed vendor assessments, implemented security controls, or obtained independent certification.

Policy requirements do not establish adoption, approval, implementation or compliance. Human review required.

2. Inventory, impact assessment and proposed schedules
Backup inventory and classification
For each dataset, record the system owner, source, business purpose, tenant scope and highest applicable
classification: Public, Internal, Confidential or Restricted under CD-ISP-001. Record the backup method,
location/account/region, copy dependencies, key identifier/version, authorized restore role, vendor and
runbook. Include coverage gaps, exclusions, deletion behavior, verification method, holds and the approval
status of proposed frequency and retention. Keep secret key material and credentials out of the backup
inventory.
Business impact analysis and objectives
System owners must prepare a business impact analysis (BIA) before recovery objectives are committed.
Assess outage harm over time, data-loss tolerance, customer and contractual obligations, dependency
failures, staffing, costs and recovery order. The Engineering Lead must review assumptions and feasibility.
The CTO approves recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO) after this assessment.
RTO is the time to restore service; RPO is the tolerable loss of recent data. Both remain TBD pending BIA,
business and contractual review. This policy provides no numerical targets or availability guarantees.
Proposed frequency and retention - TBD
Backup frequency and retention are TBD pending BIA/business and contractual review. Owners must propose
risk-based values for each dataset, considering change rate, sensitivity, loss tolerance, recovery cost and
obligations. The Engineering Lead must review them and the CTO must approve them before deployment.
Record approved values and their rationale separately. No daily, weekly or other deployed schedule or fixed
retention period is asserted. Assess snapshots and replication for recoverability independently: replication can
propagate corruption and does not by itself prove that a backup can be recovered.
Retention, holds and disposal
Reconcile backup expiry with customer deletion commitments, legal or incident holds and vendor deletion
behavior, using appropriate advice. Record delayed deletion in retained copies and prevent deleted data from
being unintentionally reintroduced during restore. Restrict held copies and their keys. Dispose of them only
after approved retention has ended and holds have been released; keep disposal evidence. Preserve the
separate minimum 12-month retention for KMS audit logs. That minimum is not a backup retention period or a
rule for all records.

3. Encryption, keys and backup protection
Encryption and grant separation
Encrypt all production backups and snapshots at rest with AES-256 and protect transfers with TLS 1.2 or TLS
1.3. Use managed KMS and backup-specific key grants separate from ordinary application access. Keep
key-encryption keys non-exportable in KMS. Separate key administration from routine data access; key
administrators receive no default decrypt permission. The Engineering Lead must approve grants. Use unique
user accounts and multi-factor authentication for administrative access. Review permissions and key grants
every quarter and revoke terminated employee access within 24 hours.
Key versions and recoverability
Rotate symmetric key-encryption keys at least every 12 months under CD-ENC-001. Rotation alone does not
re-encrypt historical data. Keep older key versions under restricted access for the full lifetime of dependent
retained backups, including legal or incident holds. Record KMS availability, account, region, identity and
version dependencies, and verify authorized decrypt access during restore checks. Never destroy a key just
because the active version has rotated. Destruction requires Engineering Lead and CTO approval, evidence
that dependent retention has ended, recovery checks showing no remaining need, and a destruction record.
Compromise and emergency access
For suspected key compromise, immediately open an incident, revoke affected identity grants and disable
compromised key versions where safe. Create replacement keys. Assess exposure, historical re-encryption
and backup recoverability before taking destructive action. The CTO must authorize temporary emergency
decrypt access, with logging and next-business-day review. Use trusted identities and recovery paths; do not
reconnect compromised grants to restore data. Review KMS administrative and decrypt audit events monthly
and after incidents. Retain those logs for at least 12 months in restricted encrypted storage.
Proposed isolation and immutability controls
Choose backup protections according to risk. Options include separate recovery identities and restricted
permission to delete backups. Consider isolated backup accounts or separate systems that would not fail
together. Provider-supported immutable copies (protected from change or deletion) or offline copies are
options where justified by risk. Before adoption, the Engineering Lead must technically verify how the provider
applies these protections, including retention locks, recovery access and cost. Test whether control of
production would let an attacker alter backups or keys. Escalate shared failure paths and document
compensating safeguards. No immutable backup, air gap, separate-region copy, geo-replication or
ransomware resistance is asserted as implemented.

CloudDesk Technologies

4. Disaster activation and safe restoration
Declaration and alternate communications
The Engineering Lead must assess disruption, affected tenants, available dependencies and likely recovery
needs using CD-IRP-001 severity rules. Escalate critical service loss, destructive activity or key/backup
compromise promptly to the CTO. The CTO must authorize disaster declaration, material service shutdowns,
resources and material residual risk. Record the scope, rationale, time and delegated authority. Follow the
incident plan for urgent reversible containment. If normal accounts or messaging are unavailable or suspect,
use separately verified alternate contacts and a restricted decision log. A human reviewer must validate
contacts and substitutes before adoption.
Dependency-led restoration sequence
System owners must document a dependency graph and propose a restoration sequence. First establish
trusted identity, administrative access, network and KMS connectivity. Then recover validated infrastructure
and configuration, restore consistent databases and objects, and reconcile queues, indexes and dependent
services. Validate and reconnect in phases. This sequence is a planning aid, not a claim about deployed
architecture. Before each step, confirm vendor prerequisites, clean credentials, backup availability, key
versions and the recovery environment. Record recovery points and dependencies. Pause if prerequisite
integrity or authorized decrypt access cannot be established.
Safe recovery after a cyber incident
Coordinate containment, evidence preservation and eradication under CD-IRP-001. Assess the compromise
window and backup provenance. Select a recovery point outside known corruption and record uncertainty.
Scan and restore in isolation with trusted tools and rebuilt systems. Remove persistence and replace
compromised credentials. A recent or decryptable backup is not proof that it is safe. Preserve incident
evidence where safe; do not overwrite originals or blindly destroy keys. The Engineering Lead verifies
containment. The CTO approves material residual risk and the return of critical service.
Tenant integrity and service gates
Before reconnection, system owners must verify hashes or application-level integrity, transactional
consistency, tenant boundaries, permissions, schema compatibility, deletion/hold reconciliation and
representative customer workflows. Reconcile replayed events and duplicate writes without exposing one
tenant to another. Record gaps, actual elapsed time and the recoverable data point. Compare these with
approved objectives when available; do not promise an unapproved RTO/RPO. Define phased monitoring,
rollback and stop criteria. Failed checks or returning indicators must stop release and reopen the investigation.
External communications require CTO authorization and a case-specific notification assessment.

[mandatory_document_context; backup_disaster_recovery_policy.pdf:p5]

CloudDesk Technologies

5. Restore testing, continuity exercises and dependencies
Representative quarterly encrypted restore tests
Test a representative encrypted restore at least quarterly. Record data integrity, authorized key access and
the recovery outcome. Plan risk-based coverage across datasets, backup types and key versions over
successive tests; this does not require restoring every backup each quarter. Use isolated environments and
synthetic data where feasible. Restrict handling of any necessary customer data. Record the source/backup
ID, recovery point, key version, operator authorization, checks, elapsed time, failures and limitations. Compare
results with approved objectives. A test is not an SLA or proof that every system can be recovered.
Negative recovery scenarios and remediation
Exercise missing or disabled keys, denied decrypt grants, unavailable KMS or providers, corrupted or
incomplete copies, inconsistent database/object recovery points, compromised credentials and cross-tenant
access attempts. Responders must stop unsafe restoration, preserve evidence and escalate to the
Engineering Lead and CTO. Use a validated alternative or document that recovery is not possible. Never
bypass authorization or suppress failed integrity checks. Assign each finding an owner and due date, and keep
retest evidence. Extracting text from this policy is not a restoration test.
Annual continuity exercises are separate
Exercise continuity scenarios at least annually and after material changes under CD-ISP-001, and coordinate
incident exercises under CD-IRP-001. Cover unavailable responders, alternate communications, cloud or
identity outages, vendor failure, ransomware, customer impact and decision authority. Record participants,
assumptions, decisions, gaps and corrective actions. An annual tabletop does not replace a representative
quarterly encrypted restore. A restore test alone does not satisfy the broader annual continuity exercise. No
exercise or restoration is claimed completed.
Vendor and shared dependencies
System owners must assess cloud storage, KMS, identity, DNS, SaaS exports, support availability, regional
dependencies and provider recovery/deletion limitations. Assess vendors before use. The Engineering Lead
must review the assessment; the CTO must accept material residual risk. Reassess critical vendors annually
and after material changes or incidents. Verify contracts, export portability, recovery responsibilities, contacts
and exit dependencies. Provider replication, assurances or advertised recovery targets do not establish
CloudDesk recoverability. Record inaccessible vendor data and recovery gaps in the risk register.

[mandatory_document_context; backup_disaster_recovery_policy.pdf:p6]
SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-BDR-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 6
CloudDesk Technologies

6. Changes, exceptions and review evidence
Change approval and risk governance
Before material changes to architecture, backup methods, retention, keys, vendors or recovery runbooks,
system owners must assess the effect on coverage and recoverability. The Engineering Lead must review
dependencies, validation and rollback. The CTO must approve material risk and revised objectives before
adoption. Update inventories and runbooks and record validation evidence. Assess risks at least annually,
before material service changes and before onboarding scoped vendors. Review open risks quarterly. The
CTO must accept residual risk; escalate overdue high-impact actions.
Exceptions and emergency deviations
Before deviating, the owner must record affected assets/data, the requirement, rationale, risk, compensating
safeguards, responsible owner and expiry. The Engineering Lead must assess the request and the CTO must
approve or reject it. Exceptions expire within 90 days and must be reviewed monthly. Renewal requires a fresh
assessment and approval. Emergency deviations require an incident record and CTO review by the next
business day. CD-ENC-001 remains authoritative for encryption exceptions and destructive key approvals.
This policy supplies no active exception or approval.
Expected evidence artifacts
Keep the backup inventory and coverage map. Keep the BIA and objective approvals, along with proposed
and approved schedules and retention.
Keep configuration and access/grant reviews. Keep backup job outcomes and failure escalations, key-version
dependency checks, restore reports and integrity results.
Keep continuity exercise findings, incident decisions and vendor assessments. Keep change and exception
approvals and corrective-action closure evidence. Restrict access to records and maintain ownership, version
history, approved retention and holds. No completed evidence artifacts are supplied. Preserve the minimum
12-month retention for KMS audit logs without applying that minimum to all records.
Human review and adoption gate
Before adoption, human reviewers must validate staffing, substitutes, declaration authority, inventories,
proposed isolation and immutability, key access and recoverability, vendor limitations, BIA, customer
contracts, notification obligations and resource feasibility. The Engineering Lead must review this policy
annually and after material changes, incidents or exercises. Record reviewer feedback and CTO approval
before operational adoption. Approval_status: not_recorded; review_status: requires_user_review. This is a
proposed policy for a fictional company, not an approved recovery plan or compliance attestation.

Policy requirements do not establish adoption, approval, implementation or compliance. Human review required.

[mandatory_document_context; incident_response_plan.pdf:p2]
SYNTHETIC / DEMO | CD-IRP-001 v1.0 | Requires user review
Page 2
CloudDesk Technologies
 Incident Response Plan
2. Reporting, classification and escalation
Proposed reporting routes
The proposed route is an access-restricted incident ticket and direct contact with the Engineering Lead
through a verified internal directory. These are proposals, not live services or monitored addresses. If
unavailable, contact the CTO or a designated substitute. If company accounts may be compromised, use a
separately verified alternate contact method. Validate contacts, coverage and escalation paths before
adoption. Report promptly when you discover a concern; do not wait for proof. Keep passwords, tokens and
unnecessary customer data out of reports.
Event versus incident
An event is an observation, such as a failed login, alert or outage, that needs assessment. An incident is
suspected or confirmed unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, destructive activity or disruption that
needs a coordinated response. The Engineering Lead records the classification and reasons, including false
positives and routine faults. If significant harm is uncertain, handle the case as a provisional incident. A lack of
confirmed exfiltration does not prove that no data was accessed.
Severity levels
SEV1 Critical: active widespread compromise, destructive cyber extortion, likely material customer data
exposure or sustained loss of a critical service. Escalate directly to the CTO and start coordinating technical
and continuity work immediately on recognition.
SEV2 High: credible privileged credential/key compromise, limited suspected customer exposure or significant

assessment. This policy provides no numerical targets or availability guarantees. Maintain reviewed continuity
and recovery procedures covering responsibilities, dependencies and communication plans. Exercise
continuity scenarios at least annually and after material changes. Record gaps and corrective actions.
Backup recovery oversight
Follow CD-ENC-001 for encrypted backups, backup-specific key grants and retention of keys needed for
recovery. Test a representative encrypted restore at least quarterly. Record integrity, authorized key access
and outcome. Owners must compare recovery results with approved continuity objectives and track gaps. This
policy provides no backup schedules, data retention periods or successful restore history.

5. Reviews, exceptions, records and enforcement
Internal security reviews
The Engineering Lead must coordinate an annual internal review of policy requirements and expected
evidence, and report findings and corrective actions to the CTO. Track owners, due dates and closure
evidence. Review open findings quarterly. Continue the quarterly access reviews and monthly KMS
administrative and decrypt audit-event reviews required by the related policies. Internal review is not an
independent audit or certification.
Exceptions and risk acceptance
Before deviating, the system owner must record affected assets and data, the requirement, rationale, risk,
compensating safeguards, owner and expiry. The Engineering Lead must assess the request; the CTO must
approve or reject it. Exceptions must expire within 90 days and be reviewed monthly. Renewal requires a fresh
assessment and approval. Emergency deviations require an incident record and CTO review by the next
business day. CD-ENC-001 remains authoritative for encryption exceptions and destructive key approvals.
This policy asserts no active exception.
Records and document control
Keep the risk register, asset inventory, assessments and approvals. Keep training records, vendor reviews
and access reviews. Also keep records of incidents, recovery exercises and findings, along with exception
tickets. Store them in an access-restricted repository with ownership, version history and approved retention
schedules. Preserve CD-ENC-001's minimum 12-month retention for KMS audit logs; that period does not
apply to all records. This policy supplies no completed evidence or approval signatures.
Enforcement and annual review
Everyone must follow approved policy requirements and report suspected violations. Managers and the CTO
must assess proportionate corrective action under applicable agreements and employment processes, with
appropriate advice. No automatic sanction is set. The Engineering Lead must review this policy annually and
after material incidents or business or technology changes. Record revisions, reviewer feedback and CTO
